_why: A guard is proven by breaking the thing it guards and watching it go red. This project does that
and writes what the guard said into the commit message - which is real, and one-time. It cannot be
re-executed. A guard proven in one month and quietly hollowed out in the next looks exactly like a
guard that still works: the suite is green either way.
This ledger is those proofs, kept as data. Each plant is the exact text substitution that puts the
defect back, and the suite that must go RED when it is there. tools/guard/replant.py applies one,
requires the named suite to fail, restores the file byte-for-byte and verifies the restore.
THREE RATCHETS, and every one of them may only fall.
owed                 registered suites with no plant at all - the honest size of what this
ledger does not cover.
owed_generalisation  plants marked site_only: the defect was put back at exactly the place it
was found, and nothing shows the guard would catch it somewhere else.
owed_real_defect     suites whose ONLY plant is marked auto. tools/guard/autoplant.py finds
those by mutating a line and watching the suite go red, which proves the
suite is not vacuous - a real thing to know, and NOT the same claim as a
hand-written plant, where the text put back is a defect that actually
happened to a user. Kept apart so a machine-generated line can never be
mistaken for the proof it is standing in for.
PlantLedgerTest holds all three to their ceilings and checks every plant still matches its file
exactly once, which is cheap; replant.py actually runs them, which is not.

plants.why: Three forms place a new record where the user is looking. Placing it at 0,0 instead drops it in a corner of a map the user may not even have on screen - and the guard that was supposed to catch this asserted the size and the script while saying nothing about x and y, because before the seam existed it could not.

plants.why: Where the centred grid image starts inside the panel was written out three times in three files, identically, and the input router had to re-derive it in screen coordinates because there was nowhere to ask. The int division is load-bearing: it goes NEGATIVE when the image is wider than the panel, which is how the grid scrolls, so a max(0,..) 'tidy' moves the picture away from the hit test.

plants.why: The matrix cursor translates a point on the grid into a cell, and the multitude/sub-chunk tool makes that grid four times finer in each axis. Dropping the multiplier makes every sub-chunk click land in the region cell instead - the same class of wrong-cell write the tool-switch defect caused, and just as silent.

plants.why: The NPC form wrote the zone and then re-read its script from that zone - and threw away the boolean saying whether the write had happened. A zone that refuses to save (a warp with no destination is the usual reason) was followed by reloading the script from a zone that had not been written, so the editor showed the old script as though it were the saved one.
plants.must_say: FAIL: AND THE SCRIPT IS NOT RE-SHOWN

The fix originally had two halves - this length-and-magic check and a catch on OutOfMemoryError - and each covered every input a suite could build, so neither could be proven while the other stood. The must_say is the section wrapper's own sentence rather than a check line: an OutOfMemoryError is not a failed assertion, it is the section dying, and what this plant proves is precisely that the editor would die.
